## Phase 8: Filesystems

**Goal.** Paths, files, directories, mounts. Then a filesystem of our own that does not have FAT's
limitations.

**Unlocks.** Loading binaries. A userspace that persists. Configuration.

**Exit gate**
- [ ] mount a FAT32 image and `ls`, `cat`, `mkdir`, `rm`, `cp` behave correctly. Reopened by the kernel review (F058, F126); lands in §10.4, and its proof mounts from a thread started with `spawn`'s 16 KiB stack.
- [x] host tests write an image through the `vibeos-core` FAT code and require host `fsck.fat -n` to report it clean, and skip that check when `fsck.fat` is not installed (F143)
- [x] `/dev`, `/proc`, and `/tmp` populated by their respective filesystems in the `Vfs` mount table, which in-guest tests and the kernel shell's `ls` reach and no syscall does (F056, F086)
- [ ] vibefs survives injected power loss during a write, verified by a crash-consistency test. Reopened by the kernel review (F014, F080); lands in §10.2 and §10.11.
- [x] path resolution in `Vfs` handles `.`, `..`, symlinks, mount point crossing, and a symlink loop, which fails with `FsError::Loop` once a walk follows more than `MAX_SYMLINK` (8) links (F056)
- [x] host tests over synthetic filesystem images, including deliberately corrupted ones
- [ ] tag `phase-8` and release `v0.8.0`

### 8.1 VFS
- [x] `Inode` with a type, size, mode, times, and link count
- [x] `Dentry` with a name-to-inode cache and negative caching
- [x] `Superblock` per mount, with a mount table and mount point crossing; §10.4's A3 box separates a mount from its superblock, so one superblock can back several mounts (DESIGN §2.11)
- [x] `FileSystem` trait for mount and root lookup; `InodeOps` for lookup, create, unlink, read, write, truncate, readdir, stat
- [x] path resolution with a bounded symlink depth
- [ ] `File` with an offset and flags, and a descriptor table that Phase 9 hands to processes. Reopened by the kernel review (F057, F086); lands in §10.4.
- [x] reference counting and a defined lifetime for an unlinked-but-open file opened through `Vfs`, which serves ramfs and kernfs files (F013, F067)
- [ ] inode and dentry caches with eviction, since an unbounded cache is a slow memory leak. Reopened by the kernel review (F065); lands in §10.4.

### 8.2 FAT32 read
- [ ] BPB parsing and validation. Reopened by the kernel review (F064); lands in §10.2.
- [x] FAT chain walking with a cluster cache
- [x] directory entry parsing, including ASCII long file names and their checksum validation (F054)
- [x] file read across cluster boundaries
- [ ] `readdir`, `stat`, timestamp conversion. Reopened by the kernel review (F123); lands in §10.4.
- [x] the on-disk structure parsing in the library half, host-tested against a generated image

### 8.3 FAT32 write
- [x] cluster allocation with a free cluster hint, FAT chain extension
- [x] file create, write, truncate, and delete through one open of a file at a time (F013)
- [x] directory create and delete, including long file name entry generation for ASCII names (F054)
- [x] both FAT copies and `FSInfo` kept in sync
- [ ] flush ordering that does not leave a directory entry pointing at unallocated clusters. Reopened by the kernel review (F013, F059); lands in §10.4 and §10.11.
- [x] verified by mounting the result on the host and running `fsck.fat`

### 8.4 Pseudo filesystems
- [x] `devfs` mounted in `Vfs`, where in-guest tests reach it: `null`, `zero`, `random`, and `urandom` nodes; `console` and `tty` nodes that read 0 bytes and reach no console until §13.7; and block-device nodes whose read and write return `NotSupp` (F081, F086)
- [ ] `tmpfs` on a private four-page instance of the Phase 7 cache type over a fixed 64 KiB store, so writes evict through the cache instead of growing a buffer; the reclaimable page-cache version is §12.5. Reopened by the kernel review (F066); lands in §10.4.
- [x] `procfs`: pid 1's directory with `cmdline`, `status`, `maps`, and `fd`, a stub; §13.9 backs `procfs` with the process table
- [x] `sysfs`-equivalent for the device tree and driver bindings
- [x] a `kernfs`-style shared implementation so the four do not duplicate directory logic

### 8.5 vibefs
- [x] the case for it: FAT32 has no permissions, no symlinks, no journaling, and no checksums, and every one of those becomes a wall
- [x] on-disk format documented in `docs/` before any code, with an explicit version field
- [ ] extent-based allocation rather than block lists. Reopened by the kernel review (F051); lands in §10.11.
- [ ] B-tree directories, so a large directory is not a linear scan. Reopened by the kernel review (F067); lands in §14.8.
- [ ] checksums on metadata and optionally on data, with corruption reported rather than propagated. Reopened by the kernel review (F063); lands in §10.11.
- [x] copy-on-write metadata updates with atomic superblock switching, chosen over a write-ahead journal in VIBEFS.md §2 (F014, F049)
- [x] snapshot create, which falls out nearly free from copy-on-write (`Vol::snapshot`, host test `snapshot_pins_generation`); §12.5 adds delete (F067)
- [x] inline data for files of at most 128 bytes, moved to an extent when a write ends past byte 128 (F062)
- [x] a host-side `mkfs` and `fsck` sharing the same format code as the kernel, so they cannot disagree
- [ ] crash consistency testing by killing QEMU at randomized points during a write workload on §10.2's volatile-cache device, then checking with `fsck` the images rebuilt from its trace. Reopened by the kernel review (F014, F080); lands in §10.2 and §10.11.

### 8.6 File API and shell
- [x] kernel-side open, read, write, seek, close, stat, readdir, mkdir, unlink, rename, symlink, link, truncate
- [ ] shell commands: `ls -l`, `cat`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm -r`, `mkdir -p`, `touch`, `stat`, `df`, `sync`. Reopened by the kernel review (F059, F126); lands in §10.4 and §10.11.
- [ ] kernel shell commands `mount` and `umount`. Reopened by the kernel review (F058, F060, F126); lands in §10.2 and §10.4.
- [x] tab completion over the current directory, which is disproportionately useful when debugging by hand
- [x] an initial ramdisk image built by the Makefile and mounted at boot, so there is a root filesystem before block drivers are trustworthy

## Phase 9: User Mode and Processes

**Goal.** Untrusted code in ring 3, isolated by hardware, talking to the kernel only through syscalls.

**Unlocks.** Everything that makes this an operating system rather than a large program.

**Exit gate**
- [x] a static ELF binary loaded from the filesystem runs in ring 3 and exits with a status the kernel reports
- [x] `write` to fd 1 from userspace reaches the console
- [x] `fork` and `exec` produce a child that runs a different binary; the parent's `wait` returns its status
- [x] a user process faulting on a bad pointer is killed with a diagnostic and does not take the kernel with it
- [x] the interactive shell runs as a user process, not in the kernel
- [ ] every pointer argument is validated: an in-guest test gives each pointer argument of `read`, `write`, `open`, `execve` (path and `argv`), `wait4` (status), and `psinfo` a kernel-half pointer, an unmapped pointer, a range that crosses `USER_END`, NULL (except `execve`'s `argv` and `wait4`'s status, which accept NULL as on Linux), and, for a pointer with a length, a huge length; every call returns `-EFAULT` and the kernel stays up. Today only `write` is tested (`syscall_ptr_validate`, `/bin/tests`), with NULL, a kernel-half pointer, an unmapped pointer, an overflowing range, and a huge length; no syscall test passes a range that crosses `USER_END`. Reopened by the kernel review (F077); lands in §10.5.

- [x] x87 and SSE state saved and restored eagerly with `fxsave64` and `fxrstor64` at syscall entry and exit and on every context switch (`switch_fpu`), which §10.6's FP binding replaces with a save at the switch away and a load before the return to ring 3, with no `xsave` and no lazy switching; the kernel itself stays soft-float on the built-in `x86_64-unknown-none` target (B2)

- [x] user mappings tracked as regions with permissions and a backing source, not just raw PTEs

- [x] teardown freeing every user frame and page table page, verified against the frame count
- [x] user pointer helpers: `AddressSpace::check_user_range` rejects a non-canonical, kernel-half, overflowing, or null-guard range and requires a present `USER` leaf on every page, and `read_bytes`, `write_bytes`, and `zero_bytes` copy through the physmap only after it passes, so a syscall given a bad pointer returns `EFAULT` without a kernel page fault (F023)
- [ ] user copies dereference the user address inside `stac`/`clac` and turn a fault into `EFAULT` through an exception-table fixup, so a write into a user page mapped without `WRITABLE` fails; today `write_bytes` ignores `WRITABLE`, and `read`, `wait4`, and `psinfo` can write into the caller's own text. Reopened by the kernel review (F023); lands in §10.6.

Reopened by the kernel review (F083); lands in §10.4.

## Phase 10: Consolidation

**Goal.** Pay down what Phase 0 laid down in a hurry, before Phase 11 adds a second architecture and
Phase 14 a userspace with a C library. The work has three sources. The 2026-09-22
[architecture review](reviews/ARCHITECTURE_REVIEW.md) has its per-item plans under
[reviews/issues/](reviews/issues/README.md), and the letter codes below name them. The
[roadmap review](reviews/ROADMAP_REVIEW.md) is the source of the entry paths and user memory, and of
the user runtime. The 2026-09-23 [kernel review](reviews/KERNEL_REVIEW.md) adds a line for
each bug it found in the code, in Phase 10 or in the later phase that first needs the fix. A finding id (Fnnn) names the plan for each line that cites it, as the letter codes do for the
issue files, and How to read this says which decides where they differ (Precedence). §10.1's CI budget,
§10.7 to §10.9 (forensics, models and proofs, and the engineering system), the §10.2 command line, and
the §10.2 deterministic build have no issue files; their boxes are the plan. All of it makes the next
three phases checkable.

**Unlocks.** A `vibeos-core` crate that a second architecture can share. A user runtime that can
express the Phase 12 and Phase 13 gates. Tables that do not cap a shell pipeline at sixteen processes.
Kernel entry and user-memory paths that copy-on-write and demand paging can build on without a
security hole. Block completions and thread-stack reclaim that Phase 13 can run on every CPU. A boot
that writes no disk it did not format. Hangs that explain themselves from the host. The seqlock, the
wake inbox, and the log ring model-checked before Phase 11 runs them on a weakly ordered CPU.

**Order.** Phase 10's parts are not all independent. `tests/gates/phase-10-needs.toml` records which
box needs which: each row names a box and the boxes it cannot be ticked before, whether its text says
so (it lands after, with, or before another) or its claim rests on them. Phase 10 lands in three
waves:

1. Wave 1 is every box in Phases 0 to 10 that cites a CRITICAL or HIGH finding without a LATENT tag
   (the set `scripts/check_review_refs.py --closed` checks: data destruction, the syscall exit and
   entry-path halts, the completion and stack-reclaim use-after-frees, the exhaustion panics, the
   vibefs and FAT leaks, and the cell soundness bounds), §10.2's box that writes every harness retry
   to the job summary, so no fix is judged by a run that retried, and every box those need through
   the needs file; `check_review_refs.py --print-wave 1` prints the set. It opens with the
   retry-summary box and §10.9's needs-file and `check_ticks.py` boxes, so every later wave-1 tick
   is checked, and with §10.1's boxes that bring `-D warnings` and clippy to the kernel's default
   build, so every later wave-1 fix is built under the standing gate, and it ends when
   `check_review_refs.py --wave 1` passes. While it is open, a Phase 10 PR merges only if its work
   is for wave-1 boxes, and a PR may tick a wave-1 box together with the boxes it needs. §10.7's
   guest core, core tool, flight recorder, tracepoint, timestamp, and `hang_test` boxes are the one
   exception: they add code, move none, and land early for the wave-1 root-causing. Until wave 1
   ends, no PR from any phase moves or renames a file under `src/`, `crates/`, `user/`, or `docs/`.
2. Wave 2 is the file moves, merged back to back with no other PR merging between the first and the
   last: A1's directory move, the moves of §10.3's arch audit, Q5's splits, the move of the in-guest
   test bodies into per-subsystem `ktest.rs` files with the runner in `src/ktest/mod.rs`, and DOC2's
   file split. Each is a pure move: outside the `mod` and `use` lines it forces, the documents that
   describe the tree, and a new check script its box names, `git diff -M --color-moved` shows only
   moved lines, and the host and in-guest test counts do not change. A box whose moves land here is
   ticked by the PR that finishes it, in this wave or the next.
3. Wave 3 is everything else, in parallel and in any order the needs file allows: among it A4's
   hooks and cycle breaks after A3, Q2's hook isolation and dead-code deletion, T1's runner protocol
   and per-test deadline after the registry runs with IF=1, §10.3's fences and `docs/ARCH.md`, and
   D2, whose PR also splits `virtio_blk_init.rs` (Q5).

A LATENT finding's fix lands in the phase its milestone names. When a Phase 10 box reaches that
milestone, the fix moves into Phase 10 and the box lands after it, or with it. §10.6's IF=1 syscall
bodies reach F033, F055, and F106, so the syscall-body box lands after §10.3's teardown box (F106),
§10.4's open-file table box (F055), and §10.6's stop-wait box (F033), which are wave 1 with it.
§10.4's path routing reaches F065 and F066, so it lands after the dentry-cache and tmpfs boxes.
§10.6's counted address space (F019) lands ahead of its milestone, Phase 12's reverse map, because
Phase 11 ports the address-space code and Phase 12's fault path, `fork`, and reverse map are written
against it.

A wave-1 fix lands in today's file layout and wave 2 moves it with the rest. Why this order: the
wave-1 bugs are live in `main` today (README), and a file move merged in the middle of them would
force every fix branch to rebase across it. Wave 1 closes under its needs because a box ticked before
the work its claim rests on has landed is the failure KERNEL_REVIEW.md §5 found most common.

- [ ] the CI budget, written into DESIGN §8.6 in the same commit as the workflow change. Every push to `main` and every pull-request update runs `check` and, alongside it, one `build` job per architecture (x86_64 now, and from Phase 11 aarch64 on the arm64 runner, which also runs `make test-unit` and the hostlib tests natively, §11.4's aarch64 switch roundtrip among them). The build job builds every ISO variant and the host `mkfs`/`fsck` tools once and uploads them. A matrix of tier jobs per architecture (`needs: [check, build]`, `fail-fast: false`, TCG) downloads them and runs the same `make test-*` targets through a prebuilt-ISO switch, so the Makefile stays the one definition of each tier. Tiers are grouped to about 40 s of QEMU each (x86_64 at `88370e5`: the five e2e boots; in-guest at `-smp 2` and `-smp 4` plus the LAPIC fallback; the vibefs crash test), and each gets its own check name, so a red PR names the failing tier. Everything else runs on a schedule: the macOS job, the KVM leg, the fuzzers, stress, and any job with a performance threshold. Later lines name two scheduled workflows, both on the pinned toolchain: the nightly job, which carries the KVM leg, and the weekly job (`smp-stress` today); the non-blocking `nightly-canary`, the one job on an undated nightly, is neither, and a line that needs its own workflow or another cadence names it (§20.8's `hardware-models`, §22.5's `fuzz.yml`, §24.2's rebuilds). A later line that says "in CI" for a functional test means a ladder tier; for a benchmark or a threshold it means the KVM leg. A red scheduled job blocks the next phase tag. The earlier no-matrix rule (runner queues) is lifted: the repository is public, so standard runners are free and unlimited, and the limits that matter are 20 concurrent jobs on the Free plan (at most 5 macOS; scheduled campaigns together hold at most 10, so pushes keep the other 10) and 6 hours per job: a scheduled run longer than 5.5 hours is split into shards that hand their state on as artifacts, and the line that needs one says so; scheduled work runs in the 10 lanes of the next box
- [ ] scheduled lanes and a ledger. Ten concurrency groups, `sched-lane-0` to `sched-lane-9`, are the scheduled share: every job on a GitHub-hosted runner of a workflow that runs on a schedule or a dispatch, `ci.yml` and `release.yml` aside, declares `concurrency: {group: sched-lane-<n>, queue: max}`, so a lane runs one job at a time and holds up to 100 waiting, first in first out, and no more than ten scheduled jobs run at once. A group without `queue: max` keeps one waiting job and cancels it when another arrives, and GitHub caps no job count across workflows, so a lane is the only queue GitHub keeps. DESIGN §8.6 holds a lane map and a ledger, changed in the same commit as the workflows they describe. The map gives each workflow its lanes, reserves for jobs that end within 5.5 hours the lanes their nightly and weekly cadence needs, which no multi-day chain (a soak, a campaign, §24.2's rebuilds) takes, and names the lanes a §22.1 release window takes. The ledger gives each scheduled or dispatched workflow's cadence, jobs per run, job-hours per run (estimated until §10.9's history measures them), peak concurrent jobs, and lanes. `scripts/check_workflows.py` fails on a scheduled or dispatched workflow with no ledger row, or with a row that puts more than 100 jobs of a run in one lane, and on a job of one with no lane or with a lane its row does not give it. `scripts/ci_history.py --budget` prints each workflow's weekly job-hours and each lane's waits, and fails when, in any of the last 4 weeks outside a release window, a lane other than §24.2's was busy more than 60% of the week, or a job in a reserved lane waited more than 12 hours to start; `--tiers` fails when a per-push tier's median QEMU time over its last 20 runs on `main` passes 60 s, which a new tier with its own check name fixes, and DESIGN §8.6 records each tier's median. `make ci-budget` runs both, and from Phase 11 an entry of `tests/gates/common.toml` (§11.7) runs that target before every phase tag. The 20 concurrent jobs are the account's, shared with its other repositories, and GitHub's Actions terms bar use that places a burden on its servers "disproportionate to the benefits provided to users", so the budget assumes the account runs no other heavy CI, and the 60% ceiling keeps the share from running full around the clock
- [ ] CI wall time cut inside each job: host packages from a cache or a prebuilt image rather than `apt-get` on every run (about 20 s of every job at `88370e5`), and independent QEMU runs in parallel inside a tier once the timing tests and the §10.2 retried failures are fixed, since concurrent QEMU under TCG makes both more likely. Push-to-green wall time is recorded in DESIGN §8.6 before and after; the aim is under two minutes for x86_64, and the box does not wait for it (3m40s at `88370e5` with no retry; a retried hang adds 60 to 90 s)
- [ ] `make debug`: QEMU `-s -S`, started through the §10.2 harness launcher, plus a `gdb` script that loads the kernel ELF and the user ELFs, documented in DESIGN §8.4
- [ ] every Linux CI job runs on GitHub's free `ubuntu-26.04` image (`ubuntu-26.04-arm` for arm64 jobs, which from Phase 11 include every job that boots an aarch64 guest, §11.7), whose apt QEMU 10.2.1 meets every QEMU minimum this file names (9.0 for the Phase 11 gate's EL2 boot and §20.1's boot with more than 255 vCPUs, 10.2 for §18.1's amd-iommu `dma-remap` and Phase 25's GHES injection) except a line that names QEMU 11.1 or later, whose jobs build that release from its tarball, checked by SHA-256 and cached by version; when `CI` is set on a Linux runner, the harness's shared QEMU launcher (§10.2) compares `qemu-system-* --version` with the version its job pins (Ubuntu's 10.2.1, or the built release) before its first boot and fails on a mismatch, so an image update that moves QEMU fails loudly; `make check`, the macOS job, and the dev host's Homebrew QEMU are left alone
- [ ] no workflow expands a `${{ }}` expression inside a `run:` script: `release.yml`'s changelog step takes the tag from `env: TAG: ${{ inputs.tag }}`, the dispatch input below, and passes `"$TAG"`, and `scripts/check_workflows.py` in `make check` fails on `${{` inside any `run:` block (F144); the same script fails on a workflow without a top-level `permissions:` block, and on any grant beyond `contents: read` that the workflow does not name a need for in a comment beside it (`ci.yml` and `smp-stress.yml` declare `contents: read`; `release.yml` declares `contents: read` and grants `actions: read` to its `build` job, which reads `ci`'s runs and the gate map's jobs through the API, and `contents: write` to its `publish` job alone, below)
- [ ] `ci.yml` runs on a push to `main` (and, from §39.3, to each supported branch), on every pull request, and on `workflow_dispatch`, never on a push to another branch. A pull request's runs share the concurrency group `ci-pr-<number>` and cancel superseded ones; every other run has a group of its own, keyed by its run id, so no run on `main` is cancelled or dropped as pending. Today every push to `main` shares one group with `cancel-in-progress`, so a merge cancels the run of the merge before it, and a fork's pull request from its own `main` joins that group. `scripts/check_workflows.py` fails on a `concurrency` group built from `github.head_ref` or `github.ref_name`, and on a workflow a §10.9 gate entry names that has no `workflow_dispatch` trigger; DESIGN §8.6 states the rule as built in the same commit
- [ ] `release.yml` publishes `vibeos.iso` alone, and publishes nothing unless a `ci` run that proves the tag's commit under §10.9's rule concluded `success`; today it runs only `make test-e2e` and also publishes `vibeos-ktest.iso`, whose block tests write fixed LBAs on any attached virtio-blk disk (F145)
- [ ] `release.yml` runs only from `main`, so the workflow that publishes, and from §14.6 signs, is always `main`'s, never a copy a tag carries from a branch cut long ago: its one trigger is `workflow_dispatch`, with the release tag as input, until §14.6 adds a `schedule` that only re-signs metadata. A `build` job with `contents: read` and `actions: read` checks through the API that the tag is annotated and points at a commit on `main` (from §22.1, or on a `release/v<x>.<m>` branch) and that a `ci` run that proves that commit under §10.9's rule concluded `success`, checks that commit out with `persist-credentials: false`, restores no cache, runs `setup.sh`, the tag tree's `make release-artifacts OUT=<dir>` (today `vibeos.iso`), and `scripts/changelog_section.py` for the notes, and uploads them with a list of their SHA-256 sums. A `publish` job with `contents: write` downloads them, checks them with `sha256sum -c`, and publishes them with the pinned release action; it checks out nothing and runs no repository script. `setup.sh` fails when `git -C limine status --porcelain --untracked-files=no` lists a changed tracked file, so a restored cache cannot change a Limine binary that the HEAD check passes (untracked files are left alone: the macOS build leaves `limine.dSYM/`); the `build` job, which restores no cache, also builds Limine's host tool fresh. `scripts/check_workflows.py` fails on `actions/cache`, a trigger other than `workflow_dispatch` (and, from §14.6, that `schedule`), or a workflow-wide write grant in `release.yml`, and on a job there with a write grant, or any job that names the `release` environment (§14.6), that checks out the repository or runs a repository script; host tests cover each rule. `docs/RELEASING.md` starts here with the owner's release steps (push the `phase-<N>` and `v0.<m>.0` tags, then dispatch `release.yml` from `main` with the release tag), and §14.6 extends it

### 10.2 Build and harness
- [x] built-in `x86_64-unknown-none` target; the custom JSON, `-Zbuild-std`, and `-Zjson-target-spec` deleted (B2)
- [x] one parametrized ISO recipe; a variant is one line (B1)

- [ ] one `target/` for every feature build: each variant's ELF is copied to a named output under `build/`, and every ISO recipe reads only its own named ELF, so a test build still cannot be packaged as production; DESIGN §8.2 and the pitfall that says "separate target directory" rewritten to that guard; `target/` is the only kernel target directory cached in CI; every ISO and ISO root is written under `build/`, so the repository root holds no build product (P1, R1)
- [x] one initrd generator; the trampoline assembled by `global_asm!` so the kernel build no longer needs `nasm` (B4); the assembly user programs still do until §10.5
- [ ] a deterministic kernel, initrd, and ISO build (moved from §17.5): a scheduled job builds every ISO variant twice from one commit, with a different checkout path, `CARGO_HOME`, and `RUSTUP_HOME` each time, and fails unless the two builds are byte-identical; §17.5's second-generation comparison and §22.1's release artifacts build on it (F151, F152)
- [ ] no build time or builder identity in the initrd or the ISO: `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` from the commit, honored by `mkinitrd` and the ISO writer; `mkiso.sh` pins staged file times and passes `-r` and `--set_all_file_dates` from `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, so Rock Ridge records no builder uid or gid; every input list sorted (F152)
- [ ] no random identifier in the ISO: fixed volume and GPT GUIDs; after `limine bios-install`, `mkiso.sh` overwrites the MBR disk signature at `0x1B8`, which Limine seeds from `time(NULL)`, with a value derived from the image; release builds record the xorriso version, which lands in the volume descriptor (F152)
- [ ] no host path in any artifact: Cargo's `trim-paths = "all"`, which passes rustc a `--remap-path-prefix` for the checkout, the sysroot, and `$CARGO_HOME`, is set for the dev and release profiles on the command line of every cargo build the Makefile runs for an artifact that ships (`-Ztrim-paths --config 'profile.<name>.trim-paths="all"'`), so panic `Location` strings, DWARF, and the ThinLTO `.llvm.<hash>` names `gen_ksyms.py` copies into `KSYMS` carry none. Those builds run on the pinned nightly, where trim-paths is unstable; no manifest carries `cargo-features = ["trim-paths"]`, which stops every stable cargo, the §10.1 MSRV step's included, from reading the workspace, and the setting moves into `Cargo.toml`'s profiles once Cargo stabilizes it (F151)
- [ ] the in-guest registry split per subsystem; a test's name and deadline printed before it runs, as `vibeOS: ktest: run <name> <deadline_ms>`, after a `vibeOS: ktest: begin <n>` that counts the boot's runs (the verdict box below); a per-test deadline in the guest, 10 s of TSC time unless the registry sets another for that test, armed as the test starts and checked on every CPU's tick, so a test that hangs with IF=0 on one CPU is still caught: the tick that finds it passed prints the failure signature `vibeOS: ktest: FAIL <name>: deadline`, registered in DESIGN §8.3, and panics, so the §10.7 dump shows where the test stood; timings read the §10.3 cycle counter, and a failure message formats into a fixed `StackBuf`, since §10.4 denies `format!`; the deadline needs the next box's IF=1 registry (T1)
- [x] the in-guest registry runs in production's interrupt context. `ktest::run` runs it on a spawned kernel thread with IF=1 and `irq_nest` 0, on a guarded 64 KiB KVA stack (the size Limine guarantees the boot stack it uses today; `spawn` gives 16 KiB), instead of on the bootstrap thread under an `InterruptGuard`, so `spawn_here` workers, which copy `irq_nest`, also run with IF=1. A test that needs interrupts off takes its own guard. `with_timer`, which runs `sti` under the registry's guard, is deleted, as is the `yield_now` in `sys_fork` with its comment about ktest's IF-off registry. In the same commit DESIGN §8.2 describes the registry's context as built, and §5.4 drops its reason that names the registry's guard. T1's per-test deadline needs IF=1. An in-guest test, `ktest_context`, fails unless it runs with IF=1, `irq_nest` 0, and its stack from `alloc_guarded_stack`, and a `spawn_here` worker it starts checks the same; on today's registry it fails. This box lands after §10.6's one ring-3 entry model box, since until then `run_user` must run on the bootstrap thread and enters ring 3 with IF=0 (F075)
- [ ] kernel stack depth is measured against DESIGN §4.5's budget: in `kernel_tests` builds, every stack a thread gets, from `spawn_inner`, AP bring-up, or reuse, is filled with a pattern, and the deepest word overwritten is found when the thread exits, before its stack is freed or reused, and for every live thread at the end of the in-guest run. The fill and the scan are portable (`vibeos-core`) with host tests, so aarch64 is measured the same way from Phase 11. At the end of a run the kernel prints one line per stack size with the deepest use seen and the thread that reached it; `run_ktest.py` writes those lines to the job summary and fails the run when a use is over its stack's budget, the stack's size minus 4 KiB, and DESIGN §8.2 documents the line in the same commit. A planted test that recurses 13 KiB deep on a 16 KiB stack runs as an expect-fail harness case, limited by `vibeos.ktest=` to that test, which passes only when the harness reports that thread over budget. - [ ] `dma::dma_mb`, a full barrier (`mfence` on x86_64) beside `dma_wmb` and `dma_rmb`, runs in `SplitQueue::should_kick` before its `avail_event` or `used.flags` load, which follows `publish`'s `avail.idx` store, and in `SplitQueue::get_used` after its `used_event` store, before the next `used.idx` load, as virtio 1.2 §2.7.13.4.1 requires and Linux's `virtio_mb` and `virtio_store_mb` provide. Today only `dma_wmb` (`fence(Release)` + `sfence`), which orders no later load, separates the `avail.idx` store from that load, and `get_used` issues no barrier after its `used_event` store, so under `VIRTIO_F_EVENT_IDX` one lost kick or interrupt stops a queue for good. A host test through the stub `arch` records ring stores, ring loads, and barriers and finds `dma_mb` between each such store and load; §11.7's litmus set covers both pairs on a weakly ordered CPU; DESIGN §4.7, §9.3, and §10.4 state the barrier as built in the same commit (F016)

### 10.4 Tables, VFS, errors
- [ ] one `limits` module in `vibeos-core` names every table and resource cap the kernel enforces as a constant, and today's fixed tables and the §10.6 exec cap take their sizes from it; the box below makes the tables heap-sized. A host test finds each fixed table's length equal to its constant (D1)
- [ ] threads, processes, descriptors, inodes, dentries, files, mounts, and regions allocated at init from a `limits` module; a cap is a constant, not a type; the in-guest test `limits_heap_backed` fills the thread, process, per-process descriptor, and region tables to their `limits` values in the default harness guest, and one entry more gets the error Linux returns: `Err` from a kernel-thread spawn, `EAGAIN` from `fork`, `EMFILE` from `open`, and `ENOMEM` from `mmap`; `scripts/check_limits.py` in `make check` fails on a `MAX_*` constant outside the `limits` module that its allowlist does not name with the hardware or on-disk bound that sizes it; each address space's regions stay a fixed table until §12.4's region tree replaces it (D1)
- [ ] the cross-CPU wake inbox holds any `ThreadId` up to the `limits` thread count (DESIGN §7.6's per-CPU bitmap of `AtomicU64` words sized from the limits, with one summary bit per word), and the KVA free-list node pool no longer caps freed thread stacks at 128 ranges; today's `u64` inbox caps ids at 64 and drops the rest silently (D1)
- [ ] a full thread table is an error, not a panic: `sys_fork` returns `EAGAIN` when §10.10's fallible `spawn_inner` finds no free slot, AP bring-up leaves a CPU offline and logs it when its idle thread or per-CPU workers find none, and `adopt_ap_idle` drops an unplaced `Box<Tcb>` only after `SCHED` is released; an in-guest test fills the thread table with parked kernel threads, then `fork` from a user program returns `-EAGAIN` (F037)
- [ ] a pid is not a table index (DESIGN §2.11 rule 4): pids and tids come from one allocator, a process's pid being its first thread's tid, in increasing order up to `pid_max` (Linux's default, 32,768, until §23.4 makes it `kernel/pid_max`), wrap to 300, Linux's `RESERVED_PIDS`, skipping ids in use, and map to their table slot through a lookup, so a reaped pid is not reused until the counter comes round. Today `proc_init::alloc_pid` hands out the lowest free slot index, so the next `fork` reuses the pid of the process just reaped, and a stale `kill` or `wait4` reaches the new process (F127). A host test allocates and frees 100 pids and sees none reused before the wrap; another marks an id as still carried by a process group after its process is reaped, and the allocator skips it at the wrap; a third, with `pid_max` at 400, allocates past it and finds the first id after the wrap is 300

### 10.5 User runtime
- [ ] a `no_std` Rust crate under `user/` as a workspace member, statically linked, with `_start`, argument and environment parsing, and a panic reported on fd 2 and turned into a non-zero exit
- [ ] built for `<arch>-unknown-linux-musl`, §24.3's user triple, as `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`, and never for a bare target: `x86_64-unknown-none` has the soft-float ABI (an `f64` multiply is a call to `__muldf3`, `f64` arguments pass in integer registers, and rustc warns that enabling SSE there breaks the target's ABI), so a native program built for it would use no SSE and could not call §14.1's C, which passes `f64` in XMM registers. The crate gets the SysV hard-float ABI, the small code model, and the prebuilt `core` and `alloc` in rustup's `rust-std` for that triple, so `-Zbuild-std` stays deleted, as B2 left it, and a `compile_error!` stops a build for any other target. It links as a static non-PIE `ET_EXEC` below 2 GiB with no `PT_INTERP`, no `DT_NEEDED`, and no crt objects, each `PT_LOAD` on pages of its own in memory and in the file (lld's `-z separate-loadable-segments`), since the loader refuses static-PIE until §13.10, through `rust-lld` and no C compiler, so the Apple Silicon dev host links it as the Linux runners do. Only the Makefile's user-crate invocation passes the flags (`-C linker=rust-lld`, `-C relocation-model=static`, `-C link-self-contained=no`, `-C link-arg=-zseparate-loadable-segments`, `-C panic=abort`), through `cargo --config`, and it keeps `-D warnings`, which a `[target]` rustflags table would otherwise shadow (F147); `.cargo/config.toml` gets no table for the triple, so §17.3's `std` builds of it keep their defaults. `memcpy`, `memmove`, `memset`, `memcmp`, and `bcmp` come from a small `#![no_builtins]` crate of the runtime, since that triple's `compiler_builtins` leaves them to a libc. `scripts/check_user_elf.py`, which the recipe runs, fails unless each user ELF is type `EXEC` with every `PT_LOAD` below 2 GiB and no `PT_INTERP` or `PT_DYNAMIC`, fails when two of its `PT_LOAD`s share a page or one is both writable and executable, and fails when one defines or calls an `f32` or `f64` soft-float helper (`__addsf3`, `__muldf3`, and the rest of compiler-rt's names). `rust-toolchain.toml`, `setup.sh`, and the CI `targets:` inputs gain `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` in the same commit, and DESIGN §3.1's table, AGENTS.md How to run, and README's toolchain line name it; Rust user code with `std` targets the same triple (§24.3)
- [ ] syscall stubs generated from one table shared with the kernel, with a number column per architecture (§11.6) and an argument order where Linux's differs by architecture (raw `clone`: arm64 swaps `tls` and `ctid`), so numbers, arities, and argument positions cannot drift; the same generator emits `docs/SYSCALL.md` §3
- [ ] syscall dispatch indexes the generated syscall table by number, taken as Linux takes it (SYSCALL.md §1: `eax` sign-extended on x86_64, the low 32 bits of `x8` unsigned on aarch64), and converts each argument to the C type the row declares for it (the width and signedness of `int`, `unsigned int`, `long`, `size_t`, `pid_t`, or a pointer), so no handler sees a bit its type does not have. The dispatcher checks no pointer itself: each handler checks a pointer where it first copies through it, after the descriptor, flag, and existence checks Linux's handler makes first (SYSCALL.md §3). Each row declares its pointer arguments (a buffer with its length argument, a fixed-size value, a C string, or a string vector); the rows for `open` (path), `execve` (path, argv, envp), and `wait4` (status) declare theirs, where `syscall.rs` gives all three a `ptr_mask` of 0 today. The declarations drive the §10.7 trace, §13.13's fuzzer, and an in-guest test that passes an unmapped and a kernel-half pointer in each declared pointer argument, with every other argument valid, and gets `-EFAULT`, so a declaration cannot drift (F150). Host tests feed the dispatcher numbers and arguments with their high 32 bits set and find each handler sees what Linux's would; in-guest, `read(-1, <unmapped>, 1)` returns `-EBADF` and `wait4` with no child and an unmapped status pointer returns `-ECHILD`

### 10.6 Entry paths and user memory
The kernel's entry paths and its user-memory copies predate copy-on-write, demand paging, and signal
return. Each item here is a live bug or a trap for Phase 12 and 13.

- [ ] user-VA accessors replace the physmap copy for syscalls. `copy_from_user` and `copy_to_user` keep the range check (canonical, above the null guard, inside the user half, no overflow), because inside `stac`/`clac` the MMU still allows supervisor access to kernel pages. They then dereference the user address inside `stac`/`clac`, so `CR0.WP` faults a write to a read-only page and a not-present page faults. A fault inside an accessor becomes `EFAULT` through an exception-table fixup, which replaces the page-table pre-walk. Today `write_bytes` writes through the physmap and ignores `WRITABLE`, so `read`, the `wait4` status pointer, and `psinfo` can write into the caller's read-only and executable pages, which Phase 12's COW would turn into cross-process corruption. An accessor reports how many bytes it copied before a fault it cannot resolve; `read`, `write`, and the other calls that return a byte count return that count when it is above 0 and `EFAULT` only when it is 0, and a call that changed state before its copy-out keeps the change (`wait4` has reaped the child) and returns `EFAULT`, as Linux's do (SYSCALL.md §5). In-guest, a 256-byte `read` of a regular file into a buffer that starts 100 bytes below an unmapped page returns 100, and a `wait4` whose status pointer is unmapped returns `EFAULT` and a second `wait4` then returns `ECHILD`. Each exception-table entry carries DESIGN §5.1's kind bit, faulting until §12.5 adds the non-faulting accessor. DESIGN §5.1, §2.5's ring-0 fault rule, the §2.7 I7 row, and SYSCALL.md §5 are rewritten in the same commit to describe the accessors as built (F023)
- [ ] no padding reaches user memory (DESIGN §2.4): the typed form of the copy-out accessor above takes only a type bounded by `zerocopy`'s `IntoBytes`, whose derive refuses at compile time a type with padding or uninitialized bytes, and its byte form takes a `&[u8]`; `zerocopy` enters with the note AGENTS.md requires. A uapi struct whose Linux layout has an implicit hole declares it as an explicit field that the kernel zeroes. A `compile_fail` doctest copies out a `#[repr(C)]` struct with a hole and fails to build. This box lands with the accessor box or after it, in its own commit
- [ ] one named fill API for writing an address space that is not running: ELF segments, zero fill, TLS, the exec stack, and `fork`'s copy until §12.3. It writes frames through the physmap and syscall code cannot reach it. It holds `PT` only to look up or install mappings, for at most one leaf table (512 entries) at a time, and copies or zeroes page contents with `PT` dropped, with IF on between chunks (DESIGN §2.9 rule 2), so a large `fork` copy does not hold off every other CPU's page-table work and its own tick for the whole copy. §12.2 teaches it to fault pages in with write intent; `scripts/check_user_access.py` in `make check` fails on a call, outside the fill-API module, to the physmap user-memory primitives it lists (today `AddressSpace::read_bytes` and `AddressSpace::write_bytes`), and on `stac` outside the accessor module
- [ ] exec returns `ENOMEM` for an image whose page-rounded `PT_LOAD` and `PT_TLS` sizes together exceed a cap in the §10.4 `limits` module that is larger than 192 MiB, so the under-cap case below exists. Today `elf::parse` checks `p_memsz` only against the user half, so one `execve` drains the buddy allocator under the PT lock with IF off. `AddressSpace::map_anon` frees what it mapped when a frame allocation fails, as the `map_page` error path does, and the loader releases the PT lock between bounded chunks. In-guest, in the default 128 MiB guest, `exec_huge_memsz`: an ELF with a 64 GiB `p_memsz` and one under the cap but larger than the guest's RAM (192 MiB of `p_memsz`) each get `ENOMEM`, which the second keeps getting after §12.2 makes loading lazy, the free-frame count returns to its baseline, and a `fork` after them succeeds (F009)
- [ ] the ELF loader maps `PT_LOAD` segments that share a page as Linux does, as a foreign binary linked with no page alignment between `.text` and `.data` has them (`ld -n`, or a linker script with no `ALIGN`): Linux maps each `PT_LOAD` after the first over the ones before it, so a shared page gets the permissions of the later segment in the program header table, which the ELF specification sorts by `p_vaddr`. The loader maps each such page once with those permissions, zero-fills it once, then copies each segment's file bytes into it, so the page holds both segments' bytes and is writable and executable only when the later segment is. Today `map_loads` takes `AsError::Overlap` as success and zeroes the earlier segment's bytes. Host tests cover an RX and an RW segment in one page, which give an RW, non-executable page holding both segments' bytes, and a pair whose second segment runs past the shared page. In-guest, a program whose RX segment starts a page before the shared page, with its entry point in that first page, reads a constant from the RX segment's tail in the shared page and a value from its data, and exits 0, and a variant that jumps into the shared page ends with `SIGSEGV`; a CI step runs the same two ELFs natively on the hosted x86_64 Linux runner and expects the same two outcomes; if Linux runs code in the shared page, or does not keep both segments' bytes there, the rule is wrong, and this box changes to what that run shows (F031)

Interrupt gates do not clear AC, ring 3 can set it with `popf`, and an IRQ or `#PF` inside an accessor would otherwise run its handler with SMAP off; `iretq` restores the interrupted value. An in-guest test opens the accessor window, takes an exception, and has a test hook in the handler make a stray access to a user page, which must fault; an x86_64-only variant does the same after a user program sets AC with `popf`; the test hook compiles only under `kernel_tests` (F088, F146)

The exit path sends a non-canonical saved RIP to `SIGSEGV` before `swapgs`, never to `iretq`. A `#GP`, `#NP`, or `#SS` whose RIP is a labeled user-return `iretq` (the syscall slow path, `vibeos_iret_user`, `vibeos_iret_user_full`, and the interrupt exit) is recognized, handled on the kernel GS, and turned into `SIGSEGV` for the process instead of `exception_halt`. An in-guest test execs an ELF whose last `PT_LOAD` page is the one below `USER_END` and ends in a `syscall`, and gets `ENOEXEC`; a `kernel_tests` hook that writes a non-canonical RIP into a syscall's saved frame finds the process killed by `SIGSEGV` and the kernel running. A new TCB starts with `fp_cpu` empty; code that writes a thread's `Tcb.fpu` empties its `fp_cpu`; code that reads the running thread's saves the live registers first, inside an `InterruptGuard`. The binding's transitions are a pure state machine in `vibeos-core`, with host tests for a migration, a reused TCB address, and a write to saved state. `make` runs `scripts/check_kernel_fp.py` on each linked kernel ELF: with the pinned toolchain's `llvm-objdump` (the `llvm-tools` component) it fails on any x87, MMX, SSE, or AVX instruction outside the FP save and load routines its allow-list names, since nothing traps a kernel FP use; `tests/harness/test_check_kernel_fp.py` covers it. DESIGN §3.1's target note, §7.5's FP row, and SYSCALL.md §1 describe the binding as built in the same commit. It lands after the syscall-exit box (F001) and the `enter_user` box (F006) above, and the F069 box below lands after it. In-guest, on one CPU: process P fills XMM0-15 with a pattern and yields in a loop while a new process Q starts, and no XMM register Q reads at its first instruction holds P's pattern; in `make test-kernel-smp4`, a `kernel_tests` hook requeues each preempted thread on the next online CPU, and a user thread that keeps a counter in `xmm0` and checks it against memory on every loop iteration runs for 2 s with no mismatch
- [ ] x86_64 user FP state follows the psABI across `fork` and `execve`, from one constant initial image: `vibeos-core` holds the psABI initial FXSAVE image as a `const` (FCW `0x037F` at bytes 0-1, MXCSR `0x1F80` at bytes 24-27, every other byte zero), and `execve`, `spawn_user`, kernel-thread creation, and `init_bootstrap` all start from it; `FPU_TEMPLATE`, `fpu_template()`, `init_fpu`'s `fninit` and `fxsave64` capture, and the `Fxsave::empty()` fallback are deleted. `sys_fork` saves the parent's live registers under the FP binding (the box above), then copies `Tcb.fpu` into the child before `make_ready`; `sys_execve`, after its point of no return, writes the constant image into `Tcb.fpu` and empties the thread's `fp_cpu`, so the return to ring 3 loads it and a switch before then saves nothing over it. SYSCALL.md §1, DESIGN §2.7's I25 row, and DESIGN §7.5 drop their F069 and F129 notes in the same commit. A host test pins the image bytes; `/bin/tests` sets MXCSR's rounding bits and `xmm0` before a `fork` and the child reads both back, and an image that `execve` starts reads MXCSR `0x1F80`, FCW `0x037F`, and `xmm0` zero; so does `/sbin/init` at its first instruction under `make test-e2e-uefi`, where OVMF may leave data in the XMM registers (F069, F129)
- [ ] console `write` holds IF=0 only for bounded work (DESIGN §2.9 rule 2): it takes the console lock once per 256-byte chunk, IF is on between chunks because the syscall body runs with IF=1 (the syscall-body box above), and the framebuffer console scrolls at most once per chunk, by min(newlines, rows) rows, from a RAM copy of the text grid, never reading VRAM back; a redraw writes at most 16 KiB of framebuffer per console-lock hold, retaking the lock for the next piece and drawing each piece from the grid as it then stands, and a line written with IF already off updates the grid and leaves the redraw to the next console write whose caller runs with IF on. Today each newline on the last row is a full-framebuffer `memmove` with IF=0, so one `write` stalls CPU 0 without bound. An in-guest test writes 4096 newlines from ring 3 while CPU 1 sees CPU 0's tick count advance (F044)
- [x] one ring-3 entry model: `/hello` and every in-guest test that enters ring 3 or binds a process run as spawned processes the kernel waits on, and the bound model is deleted: `run_path`, `run_user`, `boot_hello`, `bind_current`, `bind_probe`, `with_user_as`, `unbind_current`, `longjmp_user`, `vibeos_user_setjmp`, `vibeos_user_longjmp`, `Proc.borrowed`, the globals `USER_JMP`, `IN_USER`, `EXIT_STATUS`, and `STDOUT`, and the `p.bound` and `in_user()` branches in `finish_exit` and `SYS_EXIT` dispatch. That removes a `setjmp` called from Rust, a bound `execve` whose address space nothing tears down, and a bound exit that skips `reparent_children`. The one setjmp left is `arch/catch.rs`'s, behind its asm trampoline, and SYSCALL.md §3 drops "bound `run_user`". In-guest, a spawned program that forks and exits without waiting leaves an orphan that §10.5's reaper rule frees when it exits, since a `kernel_tests` build starts no `/sbin/init` (F082, F040, F087, F127)
- [ ] an address space is a two-count object (DESIGN §2.11): `users` counts its process's thread and any pin, a pin is taken only by get-unless-zero, and the last `users` put runs the teardown; the core, a `kalloc` `TryArc` that each region and each `users` holder references, holds the root and, from §12.1 and §12.3, the page-table lock and the CPU set, and freeing it frees the root and runs no teardown, so §10.3's teardown assertion moves to the root's free. Code reaches a space through a scoped guard (`with_current_space(|as| ..)`), never a `&'static AddressSpace`: `current_space`, `space_of`, `current_as`, `peek_user_as`, `set_user_as`, `CURRENT_AS`, and the pid-0 fallback are deleted, and the box above has already deleted `bind_current` and `Proc.borrowed`. It lands after the user-VA accessor box, the box above, and §10.4's `kalloc` box. - [ ] boot runs on a guarded stack: the kernel includes Limine's stack size request (256 KiB), and once KVA is up the bootstrap thread moves to a guarded 64 KiB KVA stack, the size §10.2 gives the registry thread, since direct calls alone reach about 32 KB from `_start` and `spawn`'s 16 KiB default would overflow. Today `_start` and all of boot run on Limine's stack, which is guaranteed only 64 KiB, has no guard page, and lies in bootloader-reclaimable memory, so an overflow writes that memory silently. An in-guest test finds the bootstrap thread's `Tcb.stack` set and the page below that stack unmapped, and DESIGN §2.4 and §9.2's guard-page rule then holds for every kernel stack. F072's third Fix item, keeping large-frame functions such as `fat_init::init` (13 KB) off the boot path, is met by this stack: DESIGN §3.5 allows a big frame on a thread with a real stack, and the guard page turns an overflow into a fault; DESIGN §4.5 names the 64 KiB bootstrap and registry stacks beside its 16 KiB default in the same commit (F072)

### 10.7 Forensics and tracing
A hang or a panic under QEMU explains itself from the host, without a rerun. It lands early: the §10.2
retry root-causing and Phases 11 to 13 debug their hangs with it.

- [ ] on a timeout, or on a panic once the kernel's dump has ended, the harness takes a guest core over QMP before it stops QEMU, when DESIGN §8.3's event rule says to: `dump-guest-memory` without `-p`, a physical ELF core with one register note per CPU (not `-z`, whose kdump format `gdb` cannot read), from which the core tool below writes the virtually addressed core that `gdb` and the §10.1 `make debug` script open, walking the page tables whose root the crashed kernel's VMCOREINFO note (below) names. A physical core describes the crashed kernel whatever each CPU's page-table root holds after a crash jump, and survives page tables the bug corrupted, where `-p` builds its mappings from every vCPU's current tables. The panic path signals `pvpanic` with the event DESIGN §2.5 steps 6 and 7 choose, and QEMU runs with `-action panic=pause`, as on aarch64 (§11.7), instead of `isa-debug-exit`, so QEMU stays up for the dump. The kernel writes the ISA `pvpanic` port only when fw_cfg, probed under §10.2's hypervisor rule, lists `etc/pvpanic-port`, and only at the port that file names, so bare metal sees no write to a guessed port; it reads the bits the device recognizes first and writes only an event among them. DESIGN §2.5, §8.3, and §8.4 describe it as built in the same commit; CI uploads a failed run's core (compressed with zstd on the host), kernel ELF, and QEMU command line as one artifact, which is public (DESIGN §1.5); a job in a workflow that names an environment or a secret uploads no core, memory dump, or QEMU command line, and `scripts/check_workflows.py` fails on one that does; the harness hands QEMU the write end of a pipe through QMP `getfd` and dumps to `fd:<name>` while zstd reads the other end, so no uncompressed core touches the runner's 14 GB disk, which a 9 GiB highmem guest's core would nearly fill; the forensics test takes one core of the highmem guest this way; if QEMU's ELF dump seeks on its output fd, so a pipe fails, that test fails, and this box then checks free space before the dump instead and skips the core, with a job-summary line, when guest RAM exceeds free space minus 2 GB
- [ ] the harness reads QEMU's QMP events and follows DESIGN §8.3's event rule: each run declares the end it expects (none, a panic, `expect=reset`, or `expect=capture`); `GUEST_PANICKED` fails a run that expects no panic after the core, ends the expected-panic e2e, and gets `cont` in an `expect=reset` run; `GUEST_CRASHLOADED` fails a run not declared `expect=capture` after a core, and an `expect=capture` run waits for the capture kernel's `vmcore: written` line and its reset; a panic signature with no event fails a run that expects no panic, with the core after `vibeOS: panic: halted` or 10 s; an `expect=reset` run boots without `-no-reboot` and fails on more QMP `RESET` events than its line expects; `expect=reset` and `expect=capture` runs take a core only when they fail. The later lines whose guest resets after a panic, a watchdog expiry, or a failed health check (§20.1's record test, the Phase 22 and Phase 30 rollback gates, and the Phase 25 reset-reason and record-cycle lines) run as `expect=reset`, and those whose panic reaches a capture kernel as `expect=capture`. Unit tests replay QMP event streams recorded from the pinned QEMU for each declaration, a `GUEST_CRASHLOADED` stream and an extra `RESET` among them, so a QEMU that pauses on `GUEST_CRASHLOADED` fails them, and the first x86_64 `q35` run shows whether fw_cfg lists `etc/pvpanic-port`. If QEMU pauses, capture runs move to `-action panic=none`; if the file is missing, x86_64 uses `pvpanic-pci` and early panics fall back to the no-event rule; neither changes the declarations or the physical cores
- [ ] a hostlib core tool reads a core with the kernel ELF, refuses with a named message a core whose VMCOREINFO `BUILD-ID` differs from that ELF's, and prints a symbolized frame-pointer backtrace for every CPU, every thread's state and saved context from the TCB table, each CPU's current thread and run queue, and the last 64 records of the §5.5 log ring; the harness prints its report after the serial tail; the report's first line is its signature, `sig: <message> @ <f0> < <f1> < <f2>`: the first line of the panic message with every number written as `N`, or `timeout` for a timeout, then the function names of the first three frames of the panicking CPU's backtrace (on a timeout, of the first CPU not in its idle loop), with no address or offset, so the same bug gives the same line in every build
- [ ] the log ring, TCB, and per-CPU types the tool reads are the portable crate's and `#[repr(C)]` (`IrqCell`, `log::Record`, `Ring`, and `Logger` are not today), with `const` assertions on their sizes and field offsets, outside `cfg(loom)`, that compile into both the kernel and the host tool, so the kernel and the host tool, built on Linux or macOS, cannot disagree, as `mkfs-vibefs` and `fsck-vibefs` share vibefs's format
- [ ] one VMCOREINFO note, in Linux's `KEY=value` text format, which every reader of a dump uses: at boot the kernel writes it into its own memory and, when QEMU's `vmcoreinfo` device is present (fw_cfg's `etc/vmcoreinfo`, probed under §10.2's hypervisor rule and written through fw_cfg's DMA interface), gives the device the note's physical address, so `dump-guest-memory` copies it into every core. It carries `BUILD-ID`, the kernel ELF's GNU build-id note, which the link gains with `--build-id`, and on x86_64 the physical address of the kernel's page-table root and its level count; §11.7 adds aarch64's root, §18.2 `KERNELOFFSET`, and §25.4 the layout entries its filter reads. A kernel entered through the crash path (§25.4) never writes the device, as Linux's fw_cfg driver skips it in a kdump kernel, so a core taken after a crash jump still describes the crashed kernel. The keys are documented in `docs/` in the same commit, as a format one build writes and another reads, and DESIGN §8.4's e2e and ktest rows gain `-device pvpanic` and `-device vmcoreinfo` on x86_64
- [ ] a flight recorder (moved from §19.1): a per-CPU ring of fixed-size records (timestamp, CPU, event, two arguments); each CPU writes only its own ring, with interrupts off for the few stores a record takes, so no lock is taken; the NMI, `#MC`, and `#DB` handlers do not record, since `cli` does not mask them, and each record carries a sequence number so the tool drops a torn last record; it is on in every build, so a hang of the production ISO carries a trace too
- [ ] tracepoints at the boundaries that exist now: syscall entry and exit, scheduler switch and wake, IRQ entry and exit, IPI send and acknowledge, page fault, and block request submit and complete; §19.1 adds the later subsystems and per-tracepoint runtime enable
- [ ] timestamps from the §10.3 cycle counter (the invariant TSC on x86_64, §2.6); each AP measures its TSC against the BSP's at bring-up with a warp test over a shared cache line, and a registered marker reports the largest skew, which DESIGN §6.4 requires before timestamps order a trace; when the TSC is not invariant or the warp test saw any backward step (Linux's `check_tsc_warp` rule), the export orders records within each CPU only and says so, and DESIGN §6.4 gains that rule in the same commit; the core tool converts them to nanoseconds with the calibration and the warp result it reads from the core and exports every CPU's ring as one Chrome trace-event JSON timeline, which Perfetto opens; a host test checks the export's required fields
- [ ] a `hang_test` feature build in which, after `smp: done`, one CPU prints a registered `hang_test: armed` marker, takes a spinlock the others then wait on, and spins with interrupts off; `make test-forensics`, in `make test`, boots it at `-smp 4`, gives up 5 s after the marker rather than at the harness timeout, so its tier stays inside the §10.1 budget, and asserts the report and the export, so the forensics are tested the way the panic path is
- [ ] the panic dump owns COM1 through DESIGN §2.5 step 1's stop primitive, which every later path that stops the other CPUs reuses: the first CPU into `begin_dump` claims the dump before it stops anyone, and a CPU that finds it claimed by another runs the stop routine without writing; the owner sets `HALTING`, sets STOP in each other online CPU's request word and sends it the `0xFE` IPI, waits up to 100 ms of TSC time for acknowledgements, sends NMI to each CPU that has not acknowledged, and waits 10 ms more; `service_incoming` reads the request word before any slot, so a CPU in a serviced spin stops without the IPI; the stop routine saves the interrupted registers and frame pointer in a per-CPU crash-register slot, sets a `stopped` flag, acknowledges, and halts, and the dump prints each slot; the NMI handler reads and clears its CPU's request word, halts at once on a CPU already stopped, and returns at once on the dump owner when no request is pending; A4's raw serial layer (§10.3) holds `HALTING`, the owner's CPU id (the `DUMPING` flag moves there), and a `write_owner` that takes no lock and no `InterruptGuard`, and once `HALTING` is set a serial write or log append on any other CPU runs the stop routine instead of writing; the dump prints a registered `vibeOS: panic: cpu N stopped (ipi|poll|nmi|panic)` or `vibeOS: panic: cpu N not stopped` line for each other online CPU. Today `halt_others` returns without waiting, a CPU spinning with IF=0 never takes the IPI and writes COM1 without the TX lock, and a second CPU into `begin_dump` re-runs `Serial::init` mid-dump. DESIGN §2.3, §2.5, §2.7 (I32), §5.2, §7.6, and §8.3 describe it as built in the same commit. A `panic_test` variant at `-smp 5` panics CPUs 0 and 1 at once while CPU 2 prints a numbered line in a loop with IF=0, CPU 3 waits with IF=0 on a `SpinMutex` that CPU 0 holds, and CPU 4 spins with IF=0 in a loop that neither polls nor writes, and the dump owner sends itself an NMI IPI after its panic message; the harness finds one panic message, its backtrace, one `vibeOS: panic: halted` line, no numbered line after the first `vibeOS: panic:` line, one of CPUs 0 and 1 `stopped (panic)`, `cpu 2 stopped (poll)`, `cpu 3 stopped (poll)`, and `cpu 4 stopped (nmi)`, and the panic exit that §10.2's expect-panic e2e requires (F135)
- [ ] an exception dump's backtrace starts at the interrupted frame: the §10.6 entry stub passes the interrupted `rbp` to `dump_backtrace`. Today `exception_halt` and `exception_vec` pass their own `rbp`, so for an error-code vector (`#GP`, `#PF`, `#DF`, and the `default_err` handlers) the walk reads the interrupted RAX, which LLVM's x86-interrupt prologue pushes at `[rbp+8]`, as a return address, and the `regs: rbp=` line shows the handler's value. The `gp_test` e2e boot faults in a function that `gp_test_trip` calls, and the harness requires the backtrace to list `gp_test_trip` and then `normal_boot_tail` (F070)
- [ ] after `begin_dump`, every panic-path write to COM1, the `reentered` line included, goes through the raw serial layer's `write_owner` (A4, §10.3; DESIGN §2.5 step 1) with IF already off and no `InterruptGuard`. Today those writes take an `InterruptGuard`, so after an `irq nest underflow` panic every write fails the guard's assertion again and the dump prints `reentered` without end. A `panic_test` variant underflows `irq_nest`, and the harness finds the original panic message and the panic exit that §10.2's expect-panic e2e requires (F071)
- [ ] the panic backtrace follows `rbp` only into a known stack: the current thread's KVA stack, the recorded boot-stack bounds, or this CPU's IST and RSP0 stacks. Today `stackish()` also accepts the `ioremap` window and every address below `0x2000_0000`, so a walk can read an MMIO register that clears on read. `vibeos_syscall_entry` zeroes `rbp` before `call vibeos_syscall_stub`, so the chain ends at the syscall boundary instead of following the user's `rbp`. Host tests cover the range check; an in-guest test walks the chain from inside a syscall made with a nonzero user `rbp` and stops at the entry (F139)
- [ ] the blocked-thread sweep finds lost timeouts: a thread that blocks with a deadline records it in its TCB (`ThreadState::Blocked` gains `deadline`, `FAR_DEADLINE` when there is none, as `Sleeping` already has one), and every `SWEEP_TICKS` ticks CPU 0's `schedule_inner` reports each `Blocked` or `Sleeping` thread whose recorded deadline is at least `OVERDUE_NS` past, which happens only when its timeout entry was lost or never queued. The check is a portable function over the thread table with a host test, and `TimeoutQueue::overdue` and its `overdue_scan` test are deleted. The scan runs under SCHED with interrupts off; if it measures above 20 µs at 1,024 threads under TCG, it moves to a low-priority kernel thread that scans 64 TCBs at a time. Today the sweep scans the timeout queue after `pop_expired_into` has drained every entry it could return, so it never reports, and a lateness check at pop time would report only a stall of every CPU's scheduler, which §25.5's lockup detectors report. An in-guest test blocks a thread with a 100 ms deadline, removes its timeout entry through a `kernel_tests` hook, and finds `sched: overdue tid <id>` within 8 s; the harness registers that line as a failure line, which fails any run whose test does not declare it (F111)
- [ ] dead scheduler and bring-up state deleted: `relink`, which runs under `SCHED` on every schedule, with `Tcb.prev` and `Tcb.next`, which nothing reads, and `PerCpu.ready_head`, which only the `per_cpu_bsp` in-guest test reads; `PerCpu.tsc_per_ms`, which only the `per_cpu_identity` in-guest test reads; and the trampoline's `PARAM_IDT` with `smp::pack_idtr`, which `smp_init` writes and the trampoline never reads; and `lock::cpu_lock_order` with its test, which nothing else calls, since DESIGN §7.7 moves threads only through inboxes, together with §4.8's line "when locking two CPU-local structures, lower `cpu_id` first". §10.2 deletes `per_cpu_bsp`'s `ready_head` assertion and its harness retry, since `ready_head` is a stale snapshot, not an invariant (F074, F111)
- [ ] syscall tracing can be switched on: `vibeos.strace=1` on the §10.2 command line calls `syscall_init::set_trace(true)`, which nothing calls today, and SYSCALL.md §6 names the option. An e2e boot with `vibeos.strace=1` finds a `user: syscall write` line for the first user `write` (F150)
- [ ] a syscall count per process: the per-TCB `syscall_count`, summed over a process's threads, is reported through syscall 500 and the `/bin/sh` `ps` built-in, which §13.9 moves to `/proc/<pid>/vibeos/syscalls`, since Linux's `/proc/<pid>/syscall` already means something else. Today nothing reads the per-TCB count. The global `SYSCALLS` counter, bumped on every entry and never read, is deleted. An in-guest test finds a process's count grown by the number of syscalls it made (F150)

### 10.8 Models and proofs
Tests sample interleavings and inputs. These cover all of them up to a stated bound, on the code the
kernel links rather than a transcription of it. They run on the host and land before Phase 11 runs the
kernel on a weakly ordered CPU.

- [ ] portable code reaches atomics, fences, and the spin-loop hint only through the §10.3 atomics seam, which is `loom`'s under `cfg(loom)`. Because `loom`'s atomics have no `const fn new`, the seam also re-exports `core`'s atomics for `static`s (`entropy`'s and `paging`'s today), which stay `core`'s under `cfg(loom)` and out of every model, and a constructor built from seam atomics (`TickClock`, `IrqCell`, `BootCell`) is `const fn` only outside `cfg(loom)`. `scripts/check_atomics.py` in `make check` fails on `core::sync::atomic` or `core::hint::spin_loop` anywhere else in the portable crate outside tests; `loom` enters as a `cfg(loom)` dev-dependency listed in the §10.9 policy
- [ ] the §10.4 wake inbox's push and drain (in `ipi_init.rs` today) and `IrqCell`, the log ring's lock (in `cell.rs`, which the portable crate compiles only for tests), move into the portable half beside the §2.7 seqlock (`TickClock`), and so do `IoWaiter`'s `done` word and the TCB's `on_cpu` flag, each as a small type whose publish and read carry their orders, taking the interrupt guard and the CPU id through the §10.3 seam, so each model runs the kernel's code; the host owner token becomes per thread (loom's `thread_local!` under `cfg(loom)`), since today every host caller is owner 1 and a contended lock reads as re-entry
- [ ] loom models: the seqlock against a writer that publishes an independent timestamp, so a torn read fails; the wake inbox with pushes from three CPUs against a drain, so no `ThreadId` is lost or delivered twice; the log ring's writers against a `dmesg` reader; the `IoWaiter` completion, `finish`'s wake and Release `done` store against `wait`'s lock-free `poll` and return, whose variant stores `done` Relaxed or before the wake; and the `on_cpu` hand-off, the switch tail's Release clear after `switch_context` returns against `spawn_inner`'s Acquire reuse check, whose variant clears it Relaxed or before `switch_context` returns. Each model has a variant with one ordering weakened or one step moved, run as a test that passes only when loom finds the failure
- [ ] `TickClock::write` bumps `seq` to odd with `fetch_add(1, Relaxed)` followed by `fence(Release)` before the payload stores, since the CPU 0 tick is its only writer, and its comment names the reader's `fence(Acquire)` that the fence pairs with. Today's `fetch_add(1, AcqRel)` orders only earlier accesses, so the C11 model lets a reader accept a new tick with an old TSC; that sequence is the seqlock model's weakened variant; the seqlock keeps two copies of its payload, a latch as DESIGN §6.4 describes, with that fence after each bump, so a reader that interrupted the writer on its own CPU reads the other copy and returns; a host test stops the writer between its two copies and finds a read returning the older value (F098)
- [ ] Kani proofs, each harness stating its bound: the buddy allocator on a 16-frame arena with orders 0 to 4, where every sequence of up to six allocate and free calls keeps allocations disjoint and aligned, the free count exact, and freed buddies merged; the §10.6 user-range check, as a pure function of `(addr, len)`, accepts exactly the non-empty ranges that do not overflow and lie wholly between the null guard and `USER_MAP_END`, and an empty range at any address below `USER_MAP_END`, the null page included, as Linux's `read(fd, NULL, 0)` needs, for every pair of 64-bit values
- [ ] `Buddy::order_for` returns `None` for a size above `PAGE_SIZE << MAX_ORDER` before it rounds. Today `next_power_of_two` overflows above 2^63: under the overflow checks both profiles set (DESIGN §3.5) it panics, and without them it would return `Some(0)` for `(1 << 63) + 1`. Host tests cover `u64::MAX` and `(1 << 63) + 1`, and a Kani harness proves that for every 64-bit `(bytes, align)` it returns `None` or an order whose block is at least `bytes` long and `align`-aligned (F103)
- [ ] Miri runs the portable crate's host tests; a test Miri cannot run is skipped under `cfg(miri)` with its reason, and each finding becomes a regression test; `miri` joins the `rust-toolchain.toml` components, so a C1 bump picks a nightly that ships it
- [ ] `make models` runs the loom models and the Kani proofs on Linux and on the Apple Silicon dev host, with `kani-verifier` at a pinned version, since Kani brings its own compiler; the nightly job runs it and Miri, and §10.2's scheduled macOS job runs `make models`
- [ ] DESIGN §8 gains a models-and-proofs tier and its routing rule: a protocol whose correctness depends on an interleaving gets a loom model, not only a stress test

### 10.9 Engineering system
Gate lines, CI timings, and dependencies as data a script reads.

### 10.10 Lifetimes and liveness
A completion's publishing store is its last access to the waiter. Deferred reclaim frees an object only
after the CPU that owns it has switched away from it. A TLB shootdown waits for every CPU's ack and never panics.

- [x] `IoWaiter::finish` makes its `done` store its last access to the waiter: under `SCHED` it runs `wake_all` on the waiter's queue, then stores `done` with Release, which `poll()` loads with Acquire. Storing `done` under `SCHED` before `wake_all` is not enough, because `wait()` returns through the lock-free `poll()` and the waiter lives on the submitter's stack. DESIGN §10.1 and a DESIGN §9.4 pitfall state the rule. An in-guest test stalls the completer at a `kernel_tests` hook just before it takes `SCHED`, and 10,000 ramdisk requests whose submitters return at once complete with no fault and no hung submitter, each write carrying a pattern unique to its LBA and sequence number and each read returning the pattern last written there, so the test also proves Phase 7's reopened line on concurrent reads and writes with no corruption; the test fails before the fix (F002)
- [ ] `thread_init::with_sched` holds an `InterruptGuard` from before it takes `SCHED` through its `place_ready` loop, so a caller that blocked itself in the closure cannot be preempted before the wakes it recorded are placed. Every closure that both blocks its caller and records a wake needs this, not only `Condvar::wait_until`: §12.6's direct reclaim wakes the writeback threads and waits, and a stopping child wakes its `WUNTRACED` parent and blocks (§13.7). DESIGN §2.9 rule 1 names this wake delivery, bounded by the fixed `places` array, and DESIGN §9.4's Condvar pitfall drops its `with_sched` sentence, both in the same commit. An in-guest test has the notifier queued on the mutex when the waiter calls `Condvar::wait`, and both finish (F034)
- [ ] a dead thread's kernel stack is reused or freed only by the CPU that ran it, after `switch_context` has moved that CPU off it: `thread_exit` parks the stack in a per-CPU slot, and the next switch tail on that CPU moves it into the CPU's stack cache (at most two stacks, as Linux's `NR_CACHED_STACKS`), which `spawn_inner` on that CPU reuses zeroed and still mapped, with no unmap and no shootdown; a stack the cache cannot take goes on a per-CPU list linked through the dead stacks themselves, which a workqueue worker on that CPU unmaps and frees with IF=1 through the §4.10 shootdown. The switch tail never unmaps, and no other CPU's `reap_zombies` touches the stack; DESIGN §4.5 and §9.2 say so. Until §12.1's categories, frame-accounting tests count cached stacks as free; §12.1 counts them as kernel stacks but leaves them out of its leak counts; either way the §10.2 quiescent baseline does not depend on which CPU ran the last exit. An in-guest test in `make test-kernel-smp4` exits 10,000 threads on CPU 0 while CPUs 1 to 3 loop through schedule tails, with no fault, no shootdown sent from a switch tail by a `kernel_tests` counter, and the free frame count back at its baseline; on the first 100 exits a `kernel_tests` hook holds the window between the store that makes the exiting thread's stack reclaimable and `switch_context` open for 10 ms of TSC time, and the test fails before the fix (F012)
- [ ] every switch tail empties the per-CPU dead-stack slot into the stack cache or the worker's list, the preempt (`from_irq`) tail included, so the slot holds at most one stack, and the global 8-entry `DEFERRED` list and its `kva: deferred free list full` panic are deleted. The in-guest test `exit_burst` exits 16 user processes back to back on one CPU, each switching to a sibling resumed from timer preemption, and the kernel stays up (F010)
- [ ] `spawn_inner` reuses a `Dead` TCB slot only when an Acquire load finds clear that thread's `on_cpu` flag, which its CPU clears with a Release store after `switch_context` returns, and `thread_exit` stores `Dead` under `SCHED`. Today the scan skips only the local CPU's current and idle threads, so a spawn on another CPU can rewrite a TCB that is still switching out. An in-guest test in `make test-kernel-smp4` spawns threads on CPUs 1 to 3 while threads exit on CPU 0, and every spawned thread runs its entry exactly once; on the first 100 exits a `kernel_tests` hook holds the window between the `Dead` store and `switch_context` open for 10 ms of TSC time, and the test fails before the fix; the flag is cleared only after every save in DESIGN §7.5's per-thread table, since §13.8's core dump and §17.4's `ptrace` requests also wait on it (F012)

An in-guest test drains the buddy allocator below the 4 frames of one kernel stack, then a kernel-thread spawn returns `Err`; `fork_oom` has a `kernel_tests` hook fail the kernel-stack allocation of a `fork`, whose `clone_full` runs first, and gets `ENOMEM` with the free-frame count back at its baseline; the kernel stays up (F010)
- [x] `wait_acks` never panics: after 1 s without every ack it keeps waiting and logs, at most once a second, a line naming the CPUs that have not acked, because `shootdown_va` and `call_mask` callers free frames as soon as it returns; a CPU that never acks becomes a hang that the §10.7 forensics report. An in-guest test in `make test-kernel-smp4` holds IF off on one CPU for 3 s of TSC time while another CPU unmaps a KVA range, and both finish; §4.10's first box drops its panic clause in the same commit; DESIGN §7.9's bounded-wait paragraph and §2.7's I31 row, which describe the 1 s panic, change in the same commit (F011)

### 10.11 Storage integrity
A filesystem or block operation that fails or is refused leaves the free count, the directory entries,
and the data checksums as it found them. The kernel writes to a disk only for a mounted filesystem or a write to its device node, and a `Flush`
covers every write whose completion was reported before it was submitted (DESIGN §10.2).

- [ ] the production kernel writes to a disk only for a mounted filesystem or a write to its device node: `stamp_vda_gpt` and its call in `part_init::init` build only with `kernel_tests`, and that build stamps only when LBA 0 to 33 and the last 33 sectors read back as zeros, never after a read error. `make test-e2e` boots the production ISO once with a 1 MiB `mkfs-vibefs` image on `vda` and once with a 1 MiB image whose only non-zero bytes are `0x55AA` at offset 510 (the entry-less MBR that `part` also finds on a whole-disk FAT32 volume), and compares each image's SHA-256 before and after. DESIGN §3.3 and §10.5 say in the same commit that only a `kernel_tests` build stamps a GPT, and only on an all-zero `vda` (F003)
- [ ] the block layer keeps only the orders DESIGN §10.2 names: `Op::Barrier`, `block_init::barrier`, `virtio_blk_init::barrier`, `cache_init::barrier`, `cache::cached_barrier`, and the queue's fence logic are deleted, along with the `barrier()` calls in the ramdisk and virtio-blk read-write in-guest tests; a `Flush` goes to the device when it is submitted and holds up no later request; `cache_init::flush` waits for each write it issues and for the writes the writeback thread already has in flight, then sends its `Flush`; `cache_init::flush` waits through a WRITEBACK state on each block-cache slot: a slot whose write is in flight keeps its key and stays readable, is never evicted or re-keyed, and takes no second write to its LBA until the first completes, a waiter sleeps on the slot's wait queue, and `flush` waits for the device's WRITEBACK slots before it sends the Flush; a write can carry `Fua`, which the block layer completes on a device without FUA by waiting for the write and then sending a `Flush`; and `src/block.rs`'s module doc states this contract. The host tests `barrier_holds_later_requests`, `flush_is_fence_then_device_op`, `no_merge_across_barrier`, and `barrier_writes_dirty_no_device_flush` are replaced: a host test on the `Queue` finds a read submitted after a `Flush` dispatched before the `Flush` completes; a host test finds a `Fua` write on a device without FUA reported complete only after a `Flush` that was dispatched after the write completed; and an in-guest test holds one `blk-wb` write at a `kernel_tests` hook and finds `cache_init::flush` send no `Flush` until the hook releases it. Another host test holds a writeback in flight, dirties the page again, and fills the cache past its size, and finds the slot still keyed, one write to that LBA in flight, no Flush sent until that write completes, and the newer data read back after it. A device class vibeOS drives that gives a filesystem no completion to wait on (virtio-blk, NVMe, and AHCI each give one), or a device found to drop its volatile cache on a reset, which §10.2's volatile-cache device can model, reopens DESIGN §10.2's contract (F015, F043)
